examples: When I first came to Japan, my heart was full of hope and anxiety.
I need to buy vegetables, meat and so on at the supermarket.
Books, clothes and other things are scattered all over the room.
What with the phone ringing and visitors coming since this morning, I can't get any rest at all.
At the graduation ceremony, I had mixed feelings, happy and sad at the same time.
What with dropping my wallet and missing the train, it's been an unlucky day.
fields.explain:
Often used in sentences with a nuance of exclamation/complaint: ～やら～やらで、… / ～やら～やらして…
More than 2 items can be used, but 2 items are most common for a natural sentence rhythm.
Compared with ～たり～たり: ～やら～やら does not emphasize alternation; it is a mixed, disorderly listing.
In formal written language, consider replacing it with ～など／～や～など.

• Lists two (or more) examples among many similar things: “what with A and B…”.
• Suggests a sense of things being out of control, messy, or of mixed feelings; usually spoken.
• The two items are usually of the same kind of meaning or the same semantic field (cluttered things, a series of mishaps, conflicting emotions...).
• Implies “there is much more” beyond the items mentioned.
fields.notes:
• “やら” was originally an old listing particle; in this pattern it is repeated to create rhythm and a nuance of “all sorts of things”.
• The forms “AやらBやらで～” and “AやらBやらして～” are very common in conversation.
• When listing conflicting emotions, the order usually follows the speaker's natural rhythm; there is no fixed rule.
meaning_vi: ￣や…など、～たり・・・たり
Equivalent to the expression tari... tari
examples: 1. 願書を出すときは、証明書を集めるやら書類に書き込むやらで大変だった。
When submitting the application, what with collecting certificates and filling in forms, it was a real hassle.
2. 10年ぶりにうちのチームが優勝した。歌うやら踊るやら、大騒ぎだった。
Our team won the championship for the first time in 10 years. There was singing and dancing; it was a huge commotion.
3. 恋人と別れた。悲しいやら寂しいやらで涙が止まらない。
I broke up with my partner. What with sadness and loneliness, I can't stop crying.
4. からの部屋は汚れた皿やら古新聞やらが散らかっていて、とても汚い。
His room is cluttered with dirty dishes, old newspapers and so on; it's really filthy. meaning_vi: What with ～ and ～ ⏐ explain: Used for listing. ⏐ examples: 1. 机の上は本やらノートやらでいっぱいだ。
The desk is covered with books, notebooks and so on.
2. この季節は、目がかゆいやら鼻水が出るやら、大変です。
In this season, what with itchy eyes and a runny nose, it's really tough.
mistakes: Using it with a neutral nuance when no emotion is intended: choose ～など/～や～など instead of ～やら～やら.
Confusing it with ～だの～だの: if there is no strong criticism, avoid ～だの～だの.
Wrong word types: keep the items consistent in type/meaning where possible so the sentence is natural; excessive mixing is confusing.
JLPT: recognize a “messy/complaining” context to choose ～やら～やら instead of ～たり～たり.

examples: Since the trains have stopped, there's no choice but to walk home.
The plan failed, so first of all we have no choice but to apologize.
The evidence is insufficient, so this time we have no choice but to let it go.
If there's no treatment, you have no choice but to live with the pain.
We are out of stock, so the only option is to give a refund.
For this problem, there is nothing but expert advice.
fields.explain:
Used when other options have been considered but none are feasible.
Has a nuance of reluctance/unwillingness; do not use it when you want to emphasize an active decision (in that case use ～ことにする/～つもりだ).
In casual speech, ～しかない is more natural; formal written language uses ～よりほかない.
Usually comes at the end of a sentence or before a noun: ～よりほかない方法／選択肢.

• Expresses a situation with only one feasible solution: “have no choice but to / the only way is…”.
• Implies a lack of initiative, a sense of being forced by objective circumstances.
• More formal than ～しかない; works well in written language and public statements.
fields.notes:
• “より” strengthens the exclusive comparison: it rules out all other options, leaving only the option before “より”.
• Often used with words such as 状況, 事情, 現実, 選択肢, 方策 to create an argumentative style.
• In company announcements: 「やむを得ず値上げせざるを得ない／値上げするよりほかない」 – a formal nuance, asking for understanding.
mistakes: Confusing it with “～つもりだ/ことにする”: if it is an active decision, do not use ～よりほかない.
Wrong form with nouns: × 努力よりほかない → ✔ 努力のほか（に）はない or Vるよりほかない.
Confusing it with ～ざるを得ない: both express reluctance, but ～ざるを得ない emphasizes “being forced”; ～よりほかない emphasizes “having no other option”.
JLPT: when the context has “他の方法がない/選択肢がない/致し方ない”, the answer leans toward ～よりほかない／～しかない／～ざるを得ない; pay attention to the formal nuance.

fields.meaning: Starting with…, first of all… | Notably…, typically…
examples: At that company, everyone from the president down to all the employees is enthusiastic about their work.
At this school, you can learn many foreign languages, starting with English.
This electronic dictionary supports many languages, including English, Spanish and Chinese.
While I was in Japan, my teacher and everyone else were truly kind to me. Thank you so much.
Recent cell phones come with various functions, starting with a camera.
In Shinjuku, many high-rise buildings stand in a row, including the Tokyo Metropolitan Government Building.
fields.explain: Used to give a typical/representative example: “first of all, there is…”. It usually lists the most prominent item first and then extends to other examples.
fields.notes:
1) Easily confused with ～など.
→ ～をはじめ is used to give a representative example at the top of a list, implying “there is much more”.
2) ～をはじめ is usually followed by other examples.
→ It often goes with など／を含め／を中心に… to extend the list.
3) Not used when simply listing everything.
→ If the list is complete/closed, this pattern is unnatural.

examples: Company A is looking for motivated people regardless of educational background (/nationality).
In this botanical garden, various flowers bloom regardless of the season.
Regardless of gender or age, many people like karaoke.
Regardless of day or night ・ regardless of whether one has experience ・ regardless of East or West
*"Part-time staff wanted. Any age. No experience required."
You can apply regardless of nationality.
fields.explain:
Formal; tends to be used in official documents/advertisements/announcements.
Usually expresses the “unrestricted scope” of a rule/condition.
Comes in the middle of a sentence and modifies the second clause; there is also the attributive form “Nを問わないN₂”.
With pairs of opposites (AかBか), it makes clear the meaning “regardless of whether A or B”.

• Regardless of/irrespective of N, what follows is still true/applies.
• Public, regulatory, slogan-like nuance: used a lot in announcements, recruitment and policies.
• Often used with classifying nouns: age, gender, nationality, weather, time, wealth, size…
• Different from “even if … still …”, which involves personal choice; this pattern states an objective scope of application.
fields.notes:
• The negative form “Nを問わないN₂” is common in job advertisements: 経験を問わない人材.
• Unnatural with direct volition/commands (do/don't) because of its objective, normative nuance.
• With nouns that do not have clear classification criteria, this pattern can be ambiguous – choose nouns with clear criteria. meaning_vi: Unrelated to ～ ⏐ explain: Indicates that the noun mentioned is unrelated to, has no influence on, and is not an issue for the following action. ⏐ examples: 1. 年齢を問わず多くの人々が集まった。
Many people gathered regardless of age.
2. 経験の有無を問わず、募集。
Recruiting regardless of whether you have experience or not.
3. 性別は問いません。
Gender does not matter.
mistakes: Confusing it with ～に関わらず: both are correct in many cases, but the JLPT often tests the formal nuance of ～を問わず.
Using it with long verb clauses: unnatural; prefer nouns/noun phrases.
Putting it in a command/volition sentence: pragmatically inappropriate.

examples: He took his hospitalization as an opportunity to quit the company.
Last year Company A changed presidents. Since then, sales have started to grow.
With the opening of the Shinkansen station, various shops opened and the area around the station became lively.
Cigarettes are going up in price soon, so I've decided to take this as an opportunity to quit.
fields.explain: ◎ Expresses the meaning "a certain event or situation becomes the reason or cause".

examples: Except for Monday
Email consultations are free except in special cases.
On weekdays except Monday, we are open until 7 p.m.
fields.notes: Expresses the meaning “treating that as an exception”. It is written-language style; in spoken language, 「－をのぞけば」 or 「…のほかは」 is more often used.

fields.meaning: After…, when… (finish the first thing, then do the next)
examples: "I will give you my answer after discussing it with my family."
I'm going to decide whether to buy it after seeing the actual item.
Unless I look into it first, I can't say anything definite.
This is a conclusion reached after discussing it many times.
"Please fill in this form and then submit it at counter No. 1."
We will make a final decision after inspecting the site.
fields.explain:
Formal; common in instructions/forms/contracts.
Meaning “after”: the first clause must be truly completed; not used for unintentional actions or actions without a clear point of completion.
Meaning “when/in terms of”: often used with words indicating difficulties/conditions such as注意,工夫,問題,課題,重要,必要.

• Meaning 1 (V-た上で): “After … then …” emphasizes completion, deliberately preparing before the next action.
• Meaning 2 (V-る上で/Nの上で): “When/In the process of …” or “In terms of …” states a condition, a point to note/difficulty/something important when carrying out an action.
• Different from “上に/上は”: “上で” is about sequence (Meaning 1) or aspect/condition (Meaning 2), not addition/affirming determination.
fields.notes:
• The phrase “～上でのN” is very common in instruction headings: 利用上の注意, 契約上の義務.
• With the meaning “after”, it often goes with verbs of evaluation/consideration: 検討する, 相談する, 確認する, 準備する.
• Meaning “in terms of”: can be replaced with “面で/観点で” in many contexts, but “上で” is more formal.
mistakes: Using V-た上で for an action without a clear point of completion → unnatural.
Confusing “上で” with “上に” (not only…but also). Their functions are completely different.
Dropping “の” in “上でのN”: writing “上でN” is wrong; it must be “上でのN”.
Using “Nの上で” for a physical location “on the surface” → the meaning becomes “in terms of”, which can easily cause misunderstanding.

examples: Now that I've taken it on, I will see it through responsibly.
If you're going to compete in the match, you should give it your all.
Now that you've decided to change jobs, put your doubts aside.
Now that the secret has leaked, we have no choice but to respond quickly.
Now that things have come to this, the only option is to consult the police.
As a student, you should fulfill your duties.
fields.explain:
Sets an established point (a decision/current situation) and infers an inevitable consequence of a normative/rule-like kind.
Has a nuance of commitment/responsibility. Suitable for work contexts and official statements.
Avoid using it to directly make the listener do something: “…上は、～してください” is unnatural.

• Expresses the idea “now that … (naturally/will) …”. From an established situation, it infers an inevitable determination/obligation/measure.
• Serious nuance, more formal than “からには”. Often used in declarations/decisions.
• The second clause is rarely a request/desire addressed to the listener; it is mainly the speaker's volition, an inevitable judgment, or a general rule.
fields.notes:
• Often accompanied by a normative conclusion: ～べきだ／～なければならない／～に違いない／～ものだ。
• “Nである上は” is less common than with verbs, but can be used when stating a position/state: 社員である上は…
• In speeches, it can be combined with “責任/覚悟/義務”: 受けた上は、責任を果たす。 explain: Expresses the reason: because ～, naturally ～. The second clause contains words expressing determination, advice, prohibition, etc.
Stiff sentence style. ⏐ examples: 1. キャプテンに選ばれた上は、がんばるしかない。
Now that I've been chosen as captain, I have no choice but to do my best.
2. 入学する上は卒業したい。
If I enter the school, I want to graduate.
mistakes: Using it to make a direct request to the listener: “…上は、～してください” → unnatural; change to “以上、よろしくお願いします” or “からには”.
The first clause is not clearly “established” (only a possibility) → logical contradiction.
Confusing it with “上で” (sequence/aspect) and “上に” (addition). “上は” is a pattern of determination/inevitability.

explain: Expresses the feeling that one naturally must ～
[以上] is followed by obligation, prohibition, request, conjecture or a strong judgment.

fields.meaning:
～した後(あと)で最後(さいご)に
After, at the end of
examples: After a long discussion, the plan was finally completed.
After a voyage lasting a month, the ship finally reached its destination.
After much hesitation, I decided to take the entrance exams for University A and University B.
After struggle upon struggle, my father died without ever seeing the experiment succeed.
"This is a conclusion reached after careful thought, so there can be no changes.
After much agonizing, I decided to quit the company.
fields.explain:
Written language; narrates a process leading to a decision/result.
“Vた末に” comes in the middle of a sentence; “Vた末、” comes at the beginning of a sentence as an adverbial.
Suggests a heavy/laborious process; not used for instantaneous events with no process.
The second clause is the final result, usually 〜ことにした／〜に至った／〜と決まった など.
fields.notes:
meaning_vi: In the end…, ultimately…
examples: 1. 家族と何度も話し合った末に、留学を決めた。
After discussing it with my family many times, I finally decided to study abroad.
2. 長い交渉の末、ようやく契約にこぎつけた。
After long negotiations, we finally managed to sign the contract.
3. 悩んだ末、手術は受けないことにした。
After agonizing over it, I decided not to have the surgery.
4. 数か月にわたる捜索の末に、行方が判明した。
After months of searching, their whereabouts were finally found.
5. 検討を重ねた末、計画は白紙に戻された。
After repeated consideration, the plan was scrapped and returned to square one.
meaning_vi: After so much… finally… (～た末に)
meaning_vi: Long after ～
explain: After going through a certain process, in the end. Often used in written language, giving a stiff sentence style.
examples: 1. 悩んだ末、進学ではなく就職することにした。
After thinking it over carefully, I decided to get a job instead of continuing my studies.
2. 住民との話し合いの末、その建物の建設は中止となった。
After discussions with residents, construction of that building was halted.
mistakes: Using it with instantaneous actions (見る・出会う) that have no process → unnatural. Use た結果/とき instead.
Confusing it with ～あげく: ～末 does not imply something bad; ～あげく usually has a negative outcome.
Choosing the wrong tense: it must be Vた + 末. Vる + 末 is not used.
Overusing it in everyday spoken language → sounds like written language; consider simplifying.
